Guidelines: Adopt standardized, interoperable communication protocols, and explicitly document topic structures, access permissions, and security configurations.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Promote the interoperability, security, and auditability of distributed systems in EdgeAI environments, ensuring that multiple — and potentially heterogeneous — components are able to communicate with reliability, predictability, and minimal ambiguity
What's problem does it address?:
"The fragmentation of communication protocols hinders interoperability among edge agents, cloud services, and embedded devices."

"The absence of formal documentation of topics, permissions, and security policies hampers testing, security validation, integration, and maintenance."

"In critical systems (e.g., healthcare, autonomous vehicles), failure to comply with such practices may lead to malfunctions or regulatory violations (such as GDPR or the AI Act)."
In what context is it applicable?:
"In EdgeAI architectures with multiple nodes and layers (cloud–edge–device)."

"In systems where sensitive data is exchanged (e.g., healthcare, smart cities, Industry 4.0)."

"In applications that demand scalability, auditability, and end-to-end security."

"Particularly critical in solutions based on ROS or MQTT, where communication is highly topic- and service-oriented."
How can be implemented?:
Adopt standard protocols such as MQTT (v5.0+), DDS, OPC-UA, or REST with support for authentication, encryption, and configurable QoS.

Document:
• The topic tree (e.g., /env/sensor/temperature), its data types, directionality (pub/sub), and periodicity.
• Permissions (who publishes, who subscribes, and under which conditions).
• Security configurations: TLS, mutual authentication, logical firewalling, etc.

For ROS, use the std_msgs message standard and tools such as rqt_graph to visualize flows; for MQTT, use ACLs and JWT-based authentication as described in security guidelines such as OWASP and RSF.
Is there any other viable way?:
Partial alternatives include:

• Defining API or message contracts informally (e.g., through comments or README files); however, this approach decreases reliability and reusability.

• Using proprietary middleware with closed protocols; nevertheless, this compromises interoperability and auditability.

The recommended best practice remains the formal standardization and documentation of such contracts.
Are there any practical examples?:
The SPENCER project, referenced in the articles “Mining guidelines for architecting robotics software” and “How do you Architect your Robots?”, standardizes messages using geometry_msgs and sensor_msgs, and explicitly defines communication channels, enabling reuse and loose coupling between modules.

    In EdgeAIBench (ICU and Smart Home), data flows between layers through well-defined structures and pipelines — documented via configuration files, with a focus on security and efficiency.

    The use of Model Cards and Data Source Cards in Kotilainen’s work (2025) enables the recording of access configurations and risk metadata in machine-readable formats — supporting secure orchestration and regulatory compliance.

Guidelines: Adopt an abstract event bus that allows switching the underlying broker or communication protocol without modifying your application code.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Facilitate the portability, maintainability, and architectural resilience of EdgeAI systems by decoupling application logic from the communication infrastructure. This fosters vendor independence, simplifies testing, and enables updates without structural impact on the application code.
What's problem does it address?:
Strong coupling between business logic and communication mechanisms (e.g., MQTT, ROS, AMQP, ZeroMQ).

Difficulty in adapting to different scenarios (cloud, fog, edge) with varying requirements (QoS, latency, privacy).

High cost of porting the application across environments with distinct brokers (e.g., from MQTT to DDS).
In what context is it applicable?:
In distributed systems where multiple nodes (communicating through topics, messages, or events) must operate in a coordinated manner."

"In edge–cloud continuum architectures with multiple levels of connectivity and availability."

"In applications where it is desirable to replace the middleware or broker (e.g., ROS 1 → ROS 2, MQTT → NATS) for reasons of performance, cost, or compatibility.
How can be implemented?:
Create an abstraction layer over the messaging bus, with interfaces such as publish(event), subscribe(topic, callback), etc.

Use frameworks that support multiple backends:
• ROS2 with RMW (ROS Middleware Abstraction) enables switching between DDS vendors such as FastDDS or CycloneDDS.
• Zenoh, Eclipse Cyclone DDS, and eProsima provide abstract layers for edge messaging.
• In Python, libraries such as event-bus, pyee, or wrappers around MQTT/NATS allow the creation of pluggable adapters.

Implement dependency injection to dynamically select the protocol at runtime (via environment variables, configuration, or service discovery).
Is there any other viable way?:
• Adapter pattern with direct binding for each protocol — although it requires recompilation and testing whenever changes occur.

• Rewriting the application for every new protocol — impractical in complex and tightly coupled systems.
Are there any practical examples?:
In Modeling Self-Adaptive IoT Architectures (Alfonso et al.), MQTT usage is encapsulated within abstract gateways and nodes, allowing the communication layer to adapt without impacting the logic of containers and services.

    ROS 2 employs rmw_implementation as a pluggable backend, enabling the replacement of CycloneDDS with FastRTPS without modifying the application code.

    In In-Edge AI (Wang et al.), the abstraction of communication between DRL agents enables operation across multiple layers (edge, fog, cloud), ensuring interoperability with diverse networks and federated brokers.

Guidelines: Implement automated health checks and load balancing mechanisms to ensure traffic is routed only to healthy service instances.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Ensure high availability, operational resilience, and quality of service (QoS) in distributed systems by guaranteeing that only active and responsive service instances receive traffic, thereby preventing cascading failures and undesired disruptions in the data flow.
What's problem does it address?:
Sending requests to unavailable services degrades user experience and undermines data collection or the execution of critical tasks.

The absence of rapid failure detection in edge instances — frequent in environments with intermittent connectivity or limited power supply.

Inefficient load balancing between edge and cloud nodes leads to local overload, remote underutilization, and non-optimized energy consumption.
In what context is it applicable?:
In architectures with multiple service instances distributed across edge, fog, and cloud devices."

"In systems that use containers, microservices, or brokers that dynamically redirect tasks."

"In applications that require continuous reliability (e.g., health monitoring, industrial automation, smart cities).
How can be implemented?:
Automated health checks:
• Implement endpoints /healthz, /readyz, or /status with liveness and readiness probes.
• Use active probes (e.g., curl, ping, grpc-health-probe) with services such as Kubernetes, Consul, Nomad, Docker Swarm, or NGINX.

Load balancing mechanisms:
• At the edge: use local proxies such as Envoy, HAProxy, or Traefik with support for active/passive health checking.
• At the core/cloud: apply load balancers such as Istio, Linkerd, or NGINX Ingress with filters based on status and latency.

Integration with circuit breakers and retries for automatic fallback (e.g., with resilience4j, Envoy, or Spring Cloud).
Is there any other viable way?:
Partial alternatives include:

• Manual or reactive external monitoring (e.g., logs combined with alerts), which does not automatically reroute traffic.

• Load balancing based solely on round-robin or priority, without considering the instance state — efficient, yet risky.

The best practice is to employ automated health checks integrated into intelligent routers or service meshes with state awareness.
Are there any practical examples?:
Kubernetes uses liveness and readiness probes to determine whether a container should be restarted or removed from traffic.

    In In-Edge AI, task redistribution in federated learning is conditioned on local failure detection, requiring continuous health checks of edge nodes.

    Edge nodes in How do you Architect your Robots? (Malavolta et al.) are frequently restarted by watchdogs and feature automatic rerouting of critical topics via ROS 2 upon failure detection.

Guidelines: Enable dynamic transport negotiation between edge and cloud components to ensure optimal communication under varying network conditions.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Adapt the communication channel and transport protocol between edge and cloud components dynamically in order to ensure performance, reliability, and energy efficiency, even under unstable network conditions such as latency variations, packet loss, or limited bandwidth.
What's problem does it address?:
Fixed protocols (e.g., TCP, MQTT, HTTP) do not always deliver optimal performance under all conditions — for instance, TCP may fail on mobile links with high packet loss."

"Edge devices may be connected through heterogeneous networks (Wi-Fi, LTE, LoRa, mesh), each with distinct characteristics and limitations."

"Inefficient communication results in energy waste, increased latency, and reduced system robustness."
In what context is it applicable?:
In distributed architectures with intermittent communication among nodes, especially in mobile, industrial, or resource-constrained environments."

"In systems that use multiple networking technologies such as Wi-Fi, 4G/5G, ZigBee, LoRaWAN, Ethernet, or mesh."

"In cases where different communication requirements coexist: low latency for alarms, high throughput for video, and reliability for critical commands.
How can be implemented?:
Runtime transport negotiation:
• Create a transport adapter with support for multiple protocols (e.g., HTTP/2, gRPC, MQTT, QUIC, WebSockets).
• Use context detection (e.g., RTT, jitter, throughput, available energy) to select the most suitable channel.
• Employ libraries such as libp2p, ZeroMQ, QUIC-Go, or NATS, which already provide native fallback/adaptability.

Incorporate policy-based decision logic:
• Rules such as: "if latency > 200 ms and jitter is high, use UDP with FEC"; "if link is stable, use gRPC with compression.

Automatic fallback with buffering:
• If the primary channel fails, switch to an alternative protocol (e.g., MQTT → HTTP REST) and resend the payload.
Is there any other viable way?:
• The use of fixed protocols with timeout and retry mechanisms — though ineffective under adverse conditions.

• Intermediate load balancers (e.g., proxies with retries or circuit breakers) may mask issues, but they do not dynamically optimize transport.

The ideal solution combines real-time adaptability with intelligent decision-making, either locally at the edge agents or through centralized control.
Are there any practical examples?:
Mobile applications alternate between QUIC/HTTP3 and MQTT depending on payload type and link quality.

    In In-Edge AI, offloading algorithms adjust transmission between devices and edge nodes based on channel conditions — reinforcing the use of adaptive layers.

    ROS 2 supports switching DDS vendors with different transport profiles and UDP multicast capabilities, which can be enabled in environments with low latency requirements or tolerable packet loss.

Guidelines: Use middleware that enables interoperability across heterogeneous systems to maintain seamless communication along the cloud–edge continuum.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Enable continuous, robust, and efficient communication among distinct software and hardware components — operating across different layers (cloud, fog, edge, devices) — through a common abstraction layer, thereby minimizing integration effort, promoting portability, and reducing coupling.
What's problem does it address?:
"Technological fragmentation: different nodes use incompatible languages, operating systems, networks, and protocols."

"Low reusability of components across platforms (e.g., edge containers do not work in the cloud without adaptation)."

"Difficulty in orchestrating, tracking, or updating distributed components across different levels of the architecture."
In what context is it applicable?:
EdgeAI systems with multiple domains and platforms (embedded devices, gateways, servers, cloud)."

"Industrial, urban, or healthcare environments with heterogeneous legacy systems and the need for secure integration."

"Solutions that must switch between components at runtime or move services across layers (e.g., edge → cloud or vice versa).
How can be implemented?:
Adopt interoperability-focused middleware:
• ROS/ROS2 with hardware abstraction and DDS support.
• Eclipse Zenoh: unified pub/sub, peer-to-peer, and store/query communication for edge–cloud.
• OPC-UA: for integration with industrial devices (sensors, PLCs, SCADA).
• gRPC with proto3: for remote calls with multi-language support and integration with service meshes.

Define a common data ontology or implement format conversion (e.g., JSON ↔ Protobuf ↔ OPC).

Use adapters and bridges (e.g., MQTT ↔ DDS, ROS ↔ OPC) to connect legacy components with modern systems.
Is there any other viable way?:
Yes, but with limitations:

• Containers exposing REST APIs can be employed for interoperability, though at the cost of increased latency and tighter coupling.

• Defining a custom protocol between components offers flexibility, but lacks scalability and reusability.

A middleware-based approach is preferable, as it supports evolution, adaptation, and compatibility across vendors and devices.
Are there any practical examples?:
The SPENCER project and other ROS-based robots utilize middlewares such as ROS 2 with DDS to harmonize sensors, maps, and logic across modules with varying computational capabilities.

    In industrial EdgeAI systems, OPC-UA is employed as the backbone for integration between IoT gateways and SCADA/ERP control systems.

    In EdgeAIBench, communication between edge and cloud is supported by a layered architecture that can be adapted with configurable middleware for multiple deployment types.

Guidelines: Enable transparent end-to-end encryption via middleware that securely intercepts communication between edge and cloud components, including traffic generated by SDKs.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Ensure the confidentiality and integrity of sensitive data throughout the entire path between Edge devices and cloud services, in a manner transparent to developers — including third-party libraries (SDKs) — by means of an intermediate security layer.
What's problem does it address?:
Embedded SDKs and libraries often generate traffic that cannot be directly controlled (e.g., HTTP APIs without TLS or with poor configuration).

The absence of end-to-end encryption may expose data in transit (e.g., biometric, sensory, or location data).

Difficulty in enforcing homogeneous security across heterogeneous architectures (different languages, operating systems, and protocols).
In what context is it applicable?:
EdgeAI environments that process critical or regulated data (healthcare, smart cities, industrial automation)."

"Systems with embedded third-party SDKs (e.g., sensor libraries, vision modules, legacy brokers)."

"Infrastructures where developers do not have full control over the entire software stack.
How can be implemented?:
Security middleware proxy:
• Insert a sidecar (e.g., Envoy, NGINX, Linkerd) that transparently intercepts traffic.
• Enable mTLS (Mutual TLS) between services, including connections generated by SDKs.

Automatic encrypted tunneling:
• Redirect all outbound connections through a secure VPN (e.g., WireGuard, Tailscale) or TLS tunnel.

Security inspection and enforcement:
• Middleware can reject insecure connections (e.g., downgrade attacks, invalid SSL) and enforce security headers.

Service mesh with transparent encryption:
• Use Istio, Consul Connect, or Kuma to apply universal mTLS and secure routing without modifying services.
Is there any other viable way?:
• Manually embedding TLS or encryption within services — functional, yet complex and difficult to maintain at scale.

• Employing point-to-point VPNs (e.g., IPsec) — effective, but rigid and with limited granular control.

A middleware- or service mesh–based approach provides security as part of the infrastructure, reducing developer dependency and ensuring consistency.
Are there any practical examples?:
Envoy Proxy intercepts HTTP calls generated by SDKs and redirects them via mTLS to cloud services.

    In federated Edge AI networks, such as in In-Edge AI or EdgeAIBench, TLS tunnels are used to secure distributed inference and gradient exchange even with embedded SDKs.

    Istio implements transparent mTLS between containers on edge and cloud nodes without requiring changes to application code.

Guidelines: Adopt a secure onboarding workflow that leverages a membership service to automatically connect new devices to edge nodes and register them with the cloud hub before initiating any data transmission.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Ensure that only trusted, authenticated, and registered devices participate in the EdgeAI architecture, establishing an initial layer of trust and traceability before any data is transmitted. This strengthens network security, facilitates identity management, and reduces risks associated with malicious or compromised devices.
What's problem does it address?:
"Devices may connect directly to the edge or cloud without undergoing formal authentication and authorization processes, which opens the door to attacks such as spoofing, sniffing, or data leakage."

"The lack of prior registration hinders the enforcement of access control policies, permission management, monitoring, and updates."

"In distributed and dynamic architectures, it is not feasible to register devices manually."
In what context is it applicable?:
In any EdgeAI architecture where new devices are dynamically added (e.g., mobile sensors, cameras, wearables).

In scenarios requiring compliance with security and privacy regulations (such as the AI Act, HIPAA, GDPR).

In solutions involving multiple domains and instances (federated environments, industries, hospitals, smart cities).
How can be implemented?:
Membership Service:
• Use a central (or federated) registration authority, such as AWS IoT Core, Azure DPS, Hyperledger Fabric CA, or a custom component.

Typical secure onboarding workflow:
• Device powers on → attempts registration via a secure channel (TLS).
• Membership service authenticates using certificate, TPM, PSK, or OTP token.
• If approved, the service registers the device in both the cloud hub and the local edge.
• Only then is traffic permitted.

Support for automatic provisioning with X.509 certificates, remote attestation, or declarative files with pre-approved UUIDs.
Is there any other viable way?:
• Registering devices manually or through the CLI — feasible in small-scale environments, but not scalable.

• Allowing automatic discovery and connection without prior verification — convenient, yet insecure and often non-compliant with regulations.

The adoption of automated workflows with strong authentication and pre-registration constitutes the ideal approach for distributed and heterogeneous environments.
Are there any practical examples?:
AWS IoT Device Provisioning uses certificates or UUIDs with predefined policies to automatically register devices in a secure hub.

    In EdgeAIBench, edge devices are integrated into a testbed that simulates onboarding via federated authentication before joining scenarios such as ICU or Smart Home.

    Hyperledger Fabric employs a certificate authority (CA) to issue digital identities before allowing peers to participate in the network — an adaptable architecture for federated EdgeAI.

Guidelines: Design and implement logical abstractions to organize and manage overlay networks across edge nodes.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Enable complex networks among Edge nodes to be organized, monitored, and adapted in a scalable and efficient manner through logical abstraction layers that are independent of the physical infrastructure or actual network topology. This facilitates intelligent routing, service discovery, segmented security, and task orchestration in distributed environments.
What's problem does it address?:
"Difficulty in managing direct connections among multiple edge nodes, especially when they are behind NATs, firewalls, or mobile networks."

"Physical topologies change frequently (shutdowns, mobility, reconfiguration), making direct routing unstable."

"The lack of abstractions prevents applications or orchestration systems from understanding the 'logical network' of collaboration among nodes."
In what context is it applicable?:
Environments with multiple Edge nodes operating in a collaborative or federated manner."

"Distributed infrastructures with unstable connectivity, NATs, firewalls, or mobility (e.g., drones, fleets, smart cities).

"Architectures that must organize nodes by roles, regions, computational capacity, or security policies.
How can be implemented?:
Logical abstraction layers:
• Create representations such as clusters, functional groups, coverage areas, or security regions.
• Use logical routing tables based on roles (e.g., leader node, sensor node, aggregator node).

Technologies for overlay networks:
• WireGuard / Tailscale / Nebula to create encrypted meshes over public or private IP.
• Libp2p / NATS / ZeroTier to form secure and adaptive P2P networks with built-in discovery.
• Kubernetes + CNI plugins (e.g., Calico, Cilium) to model overlay networks with declarative policies.

Integration with orchestrators:
• Controllers update the logical network based on real-time conditions (QoS, load, failures).
• APIs or CRDs allow querying and modifying the logical network at runtime.
Is there any other viable way?:
• Manually managing point-to-point connections — functional, but fragile, error-prone, and with limited scalability.

• Employing fixed physical networks — feasible in datacenter environments, but impractical in distributed edge scenarios.

The construction of logical overlay networks abstracts underlying complexities and facilitates mobility, scalability, and resilience.
Are there any practical examples?:
Tailscale implements secure mesh networks between edge nodes using WireGuard, with identity-based authentication.

    Libp2p (from IPFS) enables the definition of logical networks and adaptive discovery among distributed peers — already utilized in decentralized edge AI.

    KubeEdge uses abstractions such as EdgeNode, EdgeCluster, and MetadataSync to synchronize logical networks between cloud and edge.

    In EdgeAIBench, environments simulate logically segmented networks (e.g., ICU vs. Smart Home) with adaptable groupings of edge nodes for specific testing scenarios.

Guidelines: Design Edge systems using a microservices-based architecture, breaking down system functionalities into loosely coupled, independent components.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Promote modularity, scalability, reusability, and ease of maintenance in EdgeAI systems by structuring the architecture into small, independent, and decoupled components that can evolve in isolation and be deployed flexibly according to the resources available.
What's problem does it address?:
Monolithic architectures hinder the updating, testing, and selective scaling of functionalities, especially in environments with energy and connectivity constraints."

"Strong coupling among components limits portability across heterogeneous edge devices."

"Horizontal scalability or selective distribution (e.g., moving only the inference service to the edge) becomes unfeasible without modularization."
In what context is it applicable?:
In hybrid Edge–Cloud architectures with variable requirements of availability, connectivity, and computational resources."

"In environments that demand local resilience (e.g., device control even without cloud connectivity)."

"In solutions where different stakeholders develop or operate distinct parts of the system (e.g., different partners manage computer vision, control, and security)."
How can be implemented?:
Define clear service boundaries (e.g., video capture, preprocessing, inference, storage, actuator control).

Package each service in isolated containers (e.g., Docker, Podman) with well-defined APIs (e.g., REST, gRPC, MQTT).

Adopt lightweight orchestrators (e.g., K3s, KubeEdge, Balena, Open Horizon) to manage instances and dependencies at the edge.

Ensure per-service security and observability (e.g., sidecars for logging, authentication, metrics).
Is there any other viable way?:
Yes, but with limitations:

• Monolithic applications with plugins — allow some degree of extensibility, but with high coupling.

• Internal componentization through threads or processes — functional, yet requiring more manual control over dependencies, deployment, and failures.

Microservices provide a much higher degree of flexibility, which is particularly relevant in edge contexts.
Are there any practical examples?:
EdgeAIBench organizes workloads into modular pipelines (e.g., preprocessing, inference, post-processing), enabling isolated analysis and runtime reconfiguration.

    ROS 2 adopts a microservices-style architecture based on independent nodes communicating via topics — a common model in robotics and edge AI.

    In KubeEdge-based architectures, each edge node functionality (such as metadata synchronization, messaging, or logging) is implemented as a microservice, facilitating continuous updates and offline fallback.

Guidelines: Expose orchestration and communication layers between modular components to support integration workflows and automation.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Enable EdgeAI systems to be automatable, integrable, and extensible by explicitly exposing the layers responsible for orchestration and communication among modules, thereby promoting observability, interoperability, and reuse across different scenarios and domains.
What's problem does it address?:
"Manual or tightly coupled integrations hinder the composition of customized flows, process automation, monitoring, or auditing."

"Embedded and undocumented orchestrations limit the adaptability of the solution (e.g., the inability to replace one module with another serving the same function)."

"In distributed architectures, the lack of visibility into the message flow hampers testing, troubleshooting, and extensibility."
In what context is it applicable?:
In modular or microservice-based solutions, especially at the edge, where modules are executed on separate or distributed devices."

"In architectures that require event-based automation, declarative flows, and integration with external tools (e.g., CI/CD, monitoring, AI retraining)."

"In industrial, robotic, or urban environments that depend on dynamic flows between sensors, actuators, and AI modules."
How can be implemented?:
Expose orchestration APIs or brokers:
• REST/gRPC APIs (e.g., /task/start, /module/graph) or declarative MQTT interfaces (e.g., control topics).

Separate control and execution modules:
• Example: orchestrator issues commands, agents execute; communication via queues/bus (e.g., NATS, MQTT, ROS2).

Enable declarative integration:
• YAML/JSON with execution graphs, schedules, and event-based triggers.
• Support external tools via webhooks, watchers, or CLI.

Expose metrics and events:
• Each layer must emit traceable events for observability and automation tools.
Is there any other viable way?:
• Systems with embedded orchestration logic — feasible for simple solutions, but difficult to maintain or extend.

• Hardcoded point-to-point integrations — functional at first, but detrimental to scalability and reusability.

By explicitly exposing these layers, the system becomes more flexible, traceable, and extensible.
Are there any practical examples?:
KubeEdge exposes layers such as EdgeMesh (communication) and EdgeController (orchestration) via APIs and synchronized events.

    In ROS 2, the orchestration layer can be managed by tools like ros2 launch or SMACH, while communication is observable via ros2 topic, facilitating the integration and automation of robotic tasks.

    In EdgeAIBench, pipeline stages (e.g., data collection, processing, inference) can be monitored or adapted at runtime through configurable files and observable layers— a model similar to declarative flows in frameworks like Node-RED or NiFi.

Guidelines: Adopt a pub/sub messaging layer to decouple service interactions and enable scalable, event-driven communication across distributed components.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Promote an event-driven, scalable, and resilient architecture by decoupling message producers and consumers through a pub/sub bus. This facilitates the dynamic composition of services, increases fault tolerance, and enhances adaptability in distributed EdgeAI systems.
What's problem does it address?:
"Direct coupling among services (e.g., synchronous REST calls) hinders scalability, monitoring, and component replacement."

"Distributed systems must react to real-time events and often include devices with intermittent connectivity or availability."

"The lack of asynchronous communication prevents multiple consumers from processing events in parallel or a producer from sending data without knowing who is listening."
In what context is it applicable?:
"In systems with multiple data producers and consumers (e.g., sensors, actuators, AI modules, controllers)."

"In heterogeneous architectures with components written in different languages or running at different levels (device → gateway → cloud)."

"In cases requiring horizontal scalability, temporal decoupling, and asynchronous event processing (e.g., logs, inferences, alarms).
How can be implemented?:
Choose an appropriate pub/sub infrastructure:
• MQTT, Apache Kafka, NATS, Redis Streams, Google Pub/Sub, ZeroMQ, or DDS.

Define well-structured topics and payloads:
• Standardize events with schemas (e.g., JSON Schema, Protobuf, Avro).
• Establish conventions for topics (e.g., edge/sensor/temperature, events/inference/done).

Integrate with other services via brokers:
• Example: orchestrators listening on task/ready, modules publishing to metrics/usage.

Manage QoS and persistence:
• QoS (e.g., MQTT 0,1,2), message retention, replay, partitions, or durable queues depending on the broker used.
Is there any other viable way?:
• Direct calls (REST/gRPC) work in simple architectures but fail in scenarios requiring flexibility, concurrent events, or fault tolerance.

• Continuous polling can simulate reactivity, but introduces overhead and latency.

The publish/subscribe approach has been proven to be scalable, decoupled, and well-suited for dynamic and distributed systems.
Are there any practical examples?:
ROS and ROS 2 use pub/sub topics as the basis for communication between robotic nodes (e.g., /camera/image_raw, /cmd_vel).

    MQTT is widely used in IoT architectures to connect sensors, actuators, and backend services via local or cloud brokers.

    In EdgeAIBench, different pipeline stages (data collection, inference, analysis) can be organized as pub/sub nodes with buffering to enable scalability and fault tolerance.

    NATS JetStream is employed in modern edge systems for communication between lightweight containers, supporting event persistence and streaming.

Guidelines: Centralize the control and observability of Edge nodes using orchestration or management platforms exposing declarative interfaces to define and monitor system state.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Enable unified, secure, and scalable management of Edge nodes through declarative interfaces and orchestration platforms, providing real-time visibility, remote state control, and continuous automation over the lifecycle of distributed components.
What's problem does it address?:
"In distributed architectures, the lack of centralization hampers state consistency, failure detection, and update orchestration."

"Monitoring based solely on local logs or ad-hoc probes is fragile, non-scalable, and prone to silent failures."

"Manual operations across multiple nodes increase the risk of inconsistency and hinder auditing or rollback."
In what context is it applicable?:
In systems with multiple Edge nodes operating simultaneously, possibly geographically distributed."

"In environments requiring auditing, compliance, or version control, such as industries, smart cities, or healthcare networks."

"In autonomous systems that reconfigure at runtime and require an external, observable control plane."
How can be implemented?:
Adopt declarative management and orchestration platforms, such as:
• Kubernetes (with extensions such as KubeEdge, MicroK8s, k3s).
• IBM Open Horizon.
• Balena, Portainer, or custom systems via GitOps (e.g., Flux, ArgoCD).

Define the desired state with YAML/JSON files:
• Services, configurations, health check routines, available resources, limits, etc.

Expose state telemetry via APIs or events:
• For example: Prometheus, MQTT/AMQP, OpenTelemetry, or REST interfaces with status endpoints.

Enable automatic reconciliation:
• If a component fails or diverges from the desired state, the platform must act to automatically restore it.
Is there any other viable way?:
• Custom scripts and manual SSH — useful for prototypes, but unfeasible at scale.

• Fragmented dashboards with metric collection but lacking declarative action — provide visibility, yet not orchestration.

Declarative platforms offer the optimal balance between human control and safe automation, particularly in edge environments.
Are there any practical examples?: EdgeAIBench provides centralized mechanisms to observe experiments in real time, aggregating metrics by device, task, and location — highlighting the importance of centralization for scientific and operational validation.

Guidelines: Design event-driven processing pipelines with continuous synchronization between edge and cloud environments, supporting configurable data sources, processing logic, and output channels.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Enable data collected and processed at the edge to be handled in reactive streams, with continuous synchronization with the cloud for storage, inference, aggregation, or visualization, while preserving configurable flexibility to dynamically define sources, processing logic, and destinations.
What's problem does it address?:
"Batch processing or rigid flows hinder responsiveness to real-time events and make the system less adaptive."

"The absence of continuous synchronization between edge and cloud leads to data inconsistency, event loss, or delayed response to critical conditions."

"Systems with statically coded flows hinder adaptation to new devices, sensors, or analytical objectives."
In what context is it applicable?:
"In systems that process continuous streams of sensory data, images, audio, or metrics."

"In hybrid Edge–Cloud environments, where part of the logic is executed locally and part remotely."

"In cases where immediate local response is required, but history and global analysis occur in the cloud (e.g., healthcare, smart cities, Industry 4.0)."
How can be implemented?:
Adopt dataflow frameworks:
• Apache NiFi, Node-RED, Flink, StreamSets, or custom pipelines using SDKs such as RxPy, Pipes and Filters.

Separate pipeline stages:
• Sources: sensors, SDKs, APIs, files, streams.
• Processing: preprocessing, cleaning, inference, enrichment.
• Outputs: databases, alerts, dashboards, automated reactions.

Continuous synchronization:
• Edge sends incremental events (e.g., MQTT, gRPC streaming) and receives commands or updates from the cloud.
• Use checkpointing, buffering, and secure retransmission mechanisms.

Dynamic configuration:
• Pipelines defined via declarative files (YAML/JSON) or graphical interfaces for runtime reconfiguration.
Is there any other viable way?:
• Rigid pipelines or those embedded directly in code are feasible, but hinder reconfiguration, adaptation to new sensors, or tuning.

• Batch data uploads to the cloud are simple, but inadequate for applications requiring reactivity or continuous control.

Event-driven pipelines provide fast response, modular scalability, and straightforward adaptability.
Are there any practical examples?:
Node-RED implements visual pipelines with configurable blocks connecting MQTT sensors, custom logic, and HTTP/DB outputs.

    EdgeAIBench models modular and comparable pipelines where each stage (e.g., data collection, inference, transmission) can be executed at different layers — with continuous and adaptive synchronization.

    In ROS/ROS 2 architectures, nodes act as pipeline stages, exchanging messages via topics. Integration with the cloud can be achieved through bridges (e.g., ROS-MQTT, ROS-WebSockets).

    Apache NiFi enables building declarative pipelines with routing, transformation, and delivery logic to multiple destinations (e.g., cloud plus local database).

Guidelines: Use isolated modules and configurable containers as self-contained execution units for deploying business logic at the edge.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Ensure that business logic at the edge is portable, secure, configurable, and easy to maintain by encapsulating each functional unit into isolated modules or self-contained containers with independent configurations, thereby facilitating selective deployment, updates, and recovery in case of failure.
What's problem does it address?:
"The lack of isolation among functions may cause conflicts, cascading failures, or uncontrolled impacts during updates."

"Manual and non-configurable deployments increase maintenance complexity and reduce scalability."

"In edge environments, where resources are limited, it is crucial to avoid dependency overlap, memory leaks, and process interference."
In what context is it applicable?:
In Edge–Cloud architectures where different modules (e.g., inference, capture, compression, actuators) operate under distinct requirements and lifecycles."

"In environments requiring automated deployment, over-the-air (OTA) updates, rollback, or service failover."

"When multiple applications share the same edge device, requiring resource isolation and security.
How can be implemented?:
Containerize each module using tools such as Docker, Podman, or OCI runtimes:
• Example: vision-service, mqtt-gateway, model-runner, logger — each in its own container with CPU/memory limits.

Make configuration external and declarative:
• Use environment variables, YAML/JSON files, mounted volumes, or centralized configuration services (e.g., Consul, etcd).

Isolate resources:
• Apply namespaces, cgroups, and AppArmor/SELinux policies to ensure failures in one module do not affect others.

Orchestrate with edge-aware platforms:
• K3s, KubeEdge, Balena, Docker Compose, Open Horizon — to manage lifecycle and dependencies.
Is there any other viable way?:
• Running multiple scripts or processes within the same environment — functional, but with high risk of interference and limited reusability.

• Packaging everything into a single monolithic application — impractical for maintenance and scalability in distributed edge environments.

Containers or isolated modules are the widely adopted best practice, even in architectures with constrained resources.
Are there any practical examples?:
BalenaOS enables the deployment of multiple independent containers on edge devices, with update and monitoring services.

    EdgeAIBench organizes processing stages (data collection, inference, analysis) into independent units, simulating isolated and configurable deployment across nodes and layers.

    ROS 2–based architectures implement each node as a separate process, allowing logical isolation and modular replacement via ROS 2–ready containers.

    In inference solutions with TensorFlow Lite, each model can be packaged with its specific runtime in separate containers, with dedicated quantization settings or hardware allocation configurations.

Guidelines: Adopt event-driven mechanisms that listen to and act upon critical events to support secure and autonomous edge architectures.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Establish a reactive operational model in which Edge nodes can detect, respond to, and automatically adapt to critical events (e.g., failures, threats, context changes), thereby ensuring operational autonomy, real-time security, and resilience in distributed environments.
What's problem does it address?:
"The absence of reactivity undermines the ability of the Edge to operate independently from the cloud."

"Delayed responses to critical events (e.g., anomalies, intrusion attempts, power or network failures) may cause data loss, downtime, or even risks to physical safety."

"Polling-based or static script models are neither efficient nor scalable for autonomous systems."
In what context is it applicable?:
In EdgeAI systems with low-latency and high-availability requirements, operating in dynamic or adverse environments (e.g., mobility, industry, energy)."

"In autonomous environments or those with intermittent connectivity, where decisions cannot rely on the cloud."

"In cases with multiple sensors and actuators where it is necessary to detect patterns, react, and prevent failures automatically.
How can be implemented?:
Create an event engine at the Edge:
• Listen to topics, queues, or sensors directly via pub/sub, WebSockets, file watchers, GPIO triggers, etc.
• Example: on_temperature_rise, on_node_failure, on_anomaly_detected.

Associate events with safe and autonomous actions:
• Example: restart service, isolate node, generate alert, switch operation mode, enforce restriction policy.

Use reactive middlewares or frameworks:
• Node-RED, Apache Edgent, RxPy, Kafka Streams, NiFi, or orchestrators with event hooks.

Integrate with security policies:
• Define events related to authentication violations, encryption failures, or traffic anomalies.
Is there any other viable way?:
• Passive monitoring with scheduled scripts (e.g., cron jobs combined with log parsing) — useful for telemetry, but insufficient for rapid and autonomous response.

• Manual alert dashboards — only effective with human intervention, which falls short of autonomy requirements.

Reactive events are essential for truly autonomous and secure architectures.
Are there any practical examples?:
Node-RED enables the construction of visual “when event X occurs, trigger Y” rules, useful for edge gateways with local logic.

    KubeEdge allows listening to device and node events, triggering remote or local controllers based on policies.

    ROS 2 robots based on lifecycle nodes react to system events to enter safety or recovery modes.

    In EdgeAIBench, events such as “model ready,” “data received,” or “node failure” trigger transitions in the inference pipeline — reinforcing the importance of reactive models in distributed environments.

Guidelines: Implement certificate-based authentication to secure communication between system modules through verified identities.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Ensure that only authenticated entities with verified identity can communicate within the system, thereby establishing mutual trust among distributed modules (edge, fog, cloud) and protecting against spoofing, hijacking, and man-in-the-middle attacks.
What's problem does it address?:
"The lack of robust authentication allows fake or compromised devices to infiltrate the system."

"Authentication based solely on tokens, passwords, or IPs is fragile in distributed and dynamic environments."

"The absence of verifiable identity undermines access control, traceability, and trust revocation."
In what context is it applicable?:
In systems with distributed communication among multiple agents (e.g., edge nodes, cloud services, brokers, gateways)."

"In scenarios with sensitive data flows, where trust must be verified through digital identity."

"In architectures requiring dynamic revocation, auditing, and fine-grained access policy definition."
How can be implemented?:
Use X.509 certificates issued by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA):
• Generate a key pair per module (public/private) and sign it with an internal CA (e.g., Vault, cfssl) or external CA (e.g., Let’s Encrypt, AWS ACM).

Enable mTLS (mutual TLS) between services:
• Bidirectional authentication: both client and server present and validate their certificates.

Automate certificate rotation:
• With SPIRE, Vault, cert-manager, or integration with enterprise PKI.

Store certificates securely:
• Use secure storage (e.g., HSM, TPM, file system with restricted permissions).

Validate identity before any sensitive communication:
• Apply validation in REST APIs, gRPC, MQTT brokers, tunnels, and service mesh sidecars.
Is there any other viable way?:
• Static tokens or passwords — useful for prototyping, but vulnerable and difficult to rotate.

• IP allowlists or ACLs — fragile in mobile or dynamic networks.

Certificate-based authentication is widely regarded as the gold standard for securing communication across distributed systems.
Are there any practical examples?:
MQTT brokers such as EMQX and Mosquitto support mutual TLS (mTLS) with client certificate authentication to secure connections. During the TLS handshake, the client presents its X.509 certificate, which the broker verifies against a trusted Certificate Authority (CA). Only clients with valid certificates signed by the trusted CA are authorized to connect, ensuring identity verification and encrypted transport. This setup enforces strict authentication and confidentiality between clients (devices) and the broker, protecting IoT infrastructures from unauthorized access and man-in-the-middle attacks.

Service meshes like Istio, Consul Connect, and Linkerd implement automatic mTLS between services, using internally managed CA certificates to establish encrypted and authenticated communication channels without requiring application code changes.

Open Horizon uses certificates to guarantee that only trusted edge agents communicate with the cloud control plane, enforcing secure identity and access management.

EdgeAIBench considers secure, identifiable connections between modules a fundamental criterion in distributed pipelines, especially in sensitive scenarios like medical ICUs and smart home IoT, where data protection and regulatory compliance are critical.

Guidelines: Use decentralized authentication methods backed by secure hardware to verify edge device identities without relying on centralized authorities.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Establish distributed trust among Edge devices through strong and tamper-proof hardware-generated identities, thereby eliminating reliance on central servers and enabling autonomous, secure, and scalable operations in disconnected or adverse environments.
What's problem does it address?:
"In many Edge scenarios (remote, offline, critical environments), relying on a central authority for authentication is unfeasible or risky."

"Software-based identities or those stored in files may be copied or compromised."

"The absence of decentralized mechanisms makes the system less resilient to attacks, failures, or censorship."
In what context is it applicable?:
In systems operating without continuous cloud connectivity (e.g., vehicles, drones, industrial sensors).

"In environments at risk of attacks on centralized infrastructure, where authenticity must be guaranteed even offline.

"In architectures requiring distributed zero trust, with support for local revocation, P2P authentication, and spoofing resistance.
How can be implemented?:
Use secure hardware to store identities:
• TPM (Trusted Platform Module), Secure Element (SE), embedded HSMs, or TEEs (e.g., ARM TrustZone).
• Each device has a private key injected or internally generated, which is never exposed.

Adopt decentralized authentication schemes:
• Challenge–response authentication with local keys.
• Schemes such as WebAuthn/FIDO2, DID (Decentralized Identifiers), or Verifiable Credentials.

Enable peer-to-peer authentication between devices:
• Example: edge nodes validating each other’s identity based on signatures and local reputation.

Distribute trust via blockchain or DHT (optional):
• Example: registration of public identities or revocation status without a single point of control.
Is there any other viable way?:
• Certificates issued by a central CA — functional, but dependent on connectivity and lacking local resilience to compromise.

• Locally stored passwords or tokens — weak, easily replicable, and without support for secure revocation.

Decentralized approaches supported by hardware are more robust, particularly in autonomous and mission-critical architectures
Are there any practical examples?:
FIDO2 with TPM in industrial or embedded devices enables secure mutual authentication without intermediate servers.

    Edge computing nodes use hardware-derived keys to authenticate among themselves in local mesh networks (e.g., drones, cooperative vehicles).

    Nitro Enclaves and Intel SGX are used to validate edge agents' identities through remote attestation without relying on a continuous central authority.

    SPRUCE, in tactical and military edge network environments, uses Secure Elements and mutual trust among peers for autonomous authentication.

Guidelines: Implement nonce-based tokens with timestamp verification to ensure message freshness and reduce replay or flooding attack surfaces.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Ensure that each message exchanged among system components is unique and recent, thereby preventing old or duplicated messages from being maliciously reused in replay or flooding attacks. This strengthens the authenticity and integrity of communication, especially in distributed and low-latency systems.
What's problem does it address?:
"Replay attacks: an adversary intercepts valid messages and resends them, triggering unauthorized actions."

"Flooding: massive resending of valid messages out of context, consuming system resources."

"The absence of freshness verification allows systems to treat old messages as legitimate, undermining business logic, security, or consistency."
In what context is it applicable?:
Any communication between distributed modules (edge ↔ edge, edge ↔ cloud) involving critical messages or sensitive actions.

Environments with public, wireless, or open networks, where interceptions and replays are plausible.

Event-driven systems, REST/gRPC APIs, and pub/sub messaging.
How can be implemented?:
Generate tokens containing:
• Nonce (unique random number per message).
• Timestamp (time of message issuance).
• Signature or MAC (to ensure integrity and authenticity).

Validate on the receiver side:
• The timestamp must be within an acceptable time window (e.g., ± 5 seconds).
• The nonce must not have been used previously (store recent nonces within a time window).

Possible implementations:
• In APIs: JWT tokens with fields iat and jti or nonce.
• In lightweight protocols: include nonce and timestamp in MQTT, CoAP, or RPC payloads.
• Use HMAC(nonce + timestamp, secret) to authenticate short messages.

Maintain a nonce/timestamp cache per trusted origin (with timeout).
Is there any other viable way?:
• Timestamps alone — protect against replay attacks but do not ensure uniqueness.

• Signatures alone — guarantee authenticity but do not prevent message replay.

• TLS alone — secures the communication channel but not the message semantics. A nonce provides additional and more granular protection.

The combination of nonce, timestamp, and signature/authentication is the robust standard for ensuring both freshness and uniqueness.
Are there any practical examples?:
OAuth 2.0/OpenID Connect uses nonce and iat (issued at) claims to ensure that tokens are not reused.

    In industrial protocols (e.g., OPC-UA, DNP3 Secure), messages contain sequence numbers and timestamps with cryptographic protection against replay attacks.

    MQTT with signed payloads (e.g., JWT or HMAC) containing nonce and exp (expiration) helps prevent duplicate commands for actuators.

    In federated learning systems, secure aggregation protocols use nonce to ensure that updates are not reused or manipulated by internal adversaries.

Guidelines: Isolate edge workloads in secure execution environments governed by strict access policies and limited execution rights.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Protect sensitive workloads executed on Edge devices against internal or external compromise by running them in isolated environments with strict permission restrictions, controlled resource access, and limited privileges — thereby promoting execution security, damage containment, and defense in depth.
What's problem does it address?:
"Workloads running with broad permissions may be exploited by adversaries to escalate privileges, access data, or attack other local services."

"The absence of effective isolation allows failures or vulnerabilities in one module to impact the entire device."

"In Edge environments, devices generally have limited physical security, which makes logical process isolation essential."
In what context is it applicable?:
In Edge systems running sensitive workloads: AI inference, physical device control, environmental monitoring, etc.

In devices shared among multiple services, organizations, or users.

In regulated applications that require data segregation, compliance, and attestation of secure execution.
How can be implemented?:
Isolated execution environments:
• Containers with reinforced isolation: Docker with seccomp, AppArmor, SELinux, no-new-privileges, user namespaces.
• Sandboxes: gVisor, Kata Containers, Firecracker (lightweight VMs), or WebAssembly runtimes (e.g., Wasmtime, Wasmer).
• Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs): Intel SGX, ARM TrustZone, AMD SEV.

Strict access policies:
• RBAC or ABAC to control access to APIs, files, devices, and networks.
• Mount volumes as read-only, use tmpfs, and block sensitive syscalls.

Run workloads as non-privileged users:
• Specific UID/GID, restricted groups, no root privileges.

Continuous monitoring and auditing:
• Log system calls, network activity, and resource usage (via auditd, Falco, AppArmor logs).
Is there any other viable way?:
• Running processes directly as services without isolation — feasible for prototyping, but insecure in production environments.

• Using minimalist operating systems (e.g., Alpine, Distroless) reduces the attack surface, but still requires logical isolation.

The use of containers with restricted execution and security policies is the ideal and widely adopted approach for secure edge computing.
Are there any practical examples?:
AWS Greengrass enables the execution of Lambda functions at the edge with configurable permissions, isolated environments, and continuous validation.

    gVisor is used in embedded devices to isolate workloads with low overhead and strong containment.

    In architectures such as EdgeAIBench, isolating inference components in configurable containers facilitates testing with malicious or faulty loads without compromising the overall system.

    Kata Containers or Firecracker VMs run AI models with near-VM level isolation, especially in gateways orchestrating multiple parallel tasks.

Guidelines: Establish encrypted point-to-point tunnels and implement active failure detection to ensure secure and resilient communication.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Ensure that communication among distributed components (Edge, cloud, gateways) is secure, private, and fault-tolerant by establishing point-to-point tunnels with strong encryption and continuous monitoring mechanisms capable of detecting outages, delays, or connectivity degradation.
What's problem does it address?:
"Communication without encryption or through shared channels may be intercepted, manipulated, or redirected (Man-in-the-Middle)."

"Silent connectivity failures between edge and cloud nodes may result in data loss, inference delays, or unexecuted critical actions."

"The absence of active detection makes the system vulnerable to intermittent failures and progressive degradation."
In what context is it applicable?:
In EdgeAI systems with unstable, public, or wireless connections, such as 4G/5G, Wi-Fi, or LPWAN.

In architectures with direct tunnels between devices, especially when no centralized routing is available."

When mission resilience must be ensured (mission-critical, real-time, or sensitive data).
How can be implemented?:
Establish encrypted point-to-point (P2P) tunnels:
• WireGuard, OpenVPN, Tailscale, StrongSwan (IPSec).
• Ensures confidentiality, mutual authentication, and resistance to spoofing or sniffing.

Integrate with dynamic name resolution:
• Using mDNS, local DNS, or DHT for distributed peers.

Implement active fault detection:
• Keep-alive with heartbeat (e.g., MQTT, gRPC), ping intervals, or API-based health checks.
• Protocols with built-in recovery (e.g., QUIC, NATS, DDS with liveliness checks).
• Failure notifications to orchestrators or monitoring systems (e.g., Prometheus + Alertmanager).

Enable automatic failover and reconnection:
• Redirect traffic to secondary channels or dynamically reconfigure (e.g., via SD-WAN or endpoint rebind).
Is there any other viable way?:
• Unencrypted direct connections — fragile and vulnerable, strongly discouraged in production environments.

• Passive retransmission via polling — consumes bandwidth and introduces latency.

• Payload-only encryption — improves privacy but does not protect metadata or provide resilience.

The combination of tunneling and active detection offers both strong security and reactive capabilities.
Are there any practical examples?:
WireGuard is used in edge-to-edge mesh networks with permanent tunnels, public key per node, and secure routing.

    gRPC employs keepalive and reconnect backoff mechanisms to detect silent failures and automatically reconnect.

    In EdgeAIBench, tests with components disconnecting and reconnecting simulate failures and evaluate recovery via the transport layer.

    KubeEdge implements disconnection detection of edge nodes towards the cloud control plane, triggering reconnection events or automatic isolation.

Guidelines: Ensure secure and trusted communication between nodes through mutual authentication, encrypted channels, and dynamic trust revocation triggered by attestation or policy violations.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Establish a secure and verifiable communication channel among system nodes (Edge, Fog, Cloud) with mutual authentication, end-to-end encryption, and the ability to automatically revoke trust when a node is compromised or violates defined policies.
What's problem does it address?:
"The absence of mutual authentication may allow connections from fake (spoofed) or compromised nodes."

"A unilaterally encrypted channel does not protect against Man-in-the-Middle attacks."

"The lack of reactive trust revocation allows insecure agents to continue operating even after a violation has been detected (e.g., through logs or remote attestation)."
In what context is it applicable?:
"In architectures with multiple cooperative nodes (e.g., edge ↔ edge ↔ cloud), exchanging data, models, or commands."

"In systems subject to dynamic trust policies (e.g., temporary devices, multi-tenant, federated learning)."

"In environments where security, traceability, and threat isolation are critical (e.g., healthcare, industry, tactical networks)."
How can be implemented?:
Mutual Authentication (mTLS or equivalent):
• Each node has its own certificate/identity, validated reciprocally.
• Based on X.509, SPIFFE/SPIRE, or hardware-backed identity frameworks.

End-to-end encrypted channels:
• TLS 1.3, WireGuard, IPSec, gRPC, MQTT over TLS.

Dynamic trust revocation:
• Continuous attestation with TPM/TEE and policies such as: “revoke if checksum mismatch, outdated patch, resource abuse...”
• Controllers with rules: if attestation.fail or policy.breach → quarantine(node).

Integration with trust authority:
• Local or federated authority with support for revocation lists (CRL), OCSP, or MQTT/REST events for revocation.

Post-revocation isolation:
• Disconnect channel, terminate session, revoke certificate, or block message routes.
Is there any other viable way?:
• Unilateral authentication via TLS — provides partial protection but does not ensure mutual trust.

• Static list of trusted devices — inflexible and vulnerable to insider attacks or post-deployment failures.

A comprehensive approach requires mutual TLS (mTLS), secure channels, and active revocation based on context or attestation.
Are there any practical examples?:
SPIRE + SPIFFE provide identity and mutual authentication with short-lived, renewable, and policy-revocable tokens.

    KubeEdge implements bidirectional mTLS between edge and cloud, with certificate rotation and state validators.

    ROS 2 with DDS Secure can validate node identities and enforce revocation based on certificates and external policies.

    In EdgeAIBench, simulated failure scenarios can be used to revoke trust from experimental nodes — due to invalid checksums, absence of heartbeats, or anomalous behavior.

Guidelines: Establish data usage policies and adopt secure middleware that enforces contextual access control and provides end-to-end protection for streaming data.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Ensure that data transmitted among system components is protected end-to-end and accessed only by authorized entities according to context-based usage policies — such as data type, source, time, purpose, or location — thereby promoting privacy, compliance, and dynamic security in distributed environments.
What's problem does it address?:
"Streaming data (such as video, sensors, or continuous inference) is often transmitted in real time without granular control, exposing risks of unauthorized access."

"Systems with static or centralized authorization cannot enforce adaptive policies across multiple consumers or dynamic scenarios."

"The absence of secure middleware hampers the consistent enforcement of usage policies across multiple modules and layers (edge, fog, cloud)."
In what context is it applicable?:
In EdgeAI systems that process and transmit sensitive or personal data: video, voice, biometrics, telemetry, clinical logs, etc."

"In environments with multiple data consumers (e.g., dashboards, cloud analytics, concurrent AI models)."

"In federated or multi-tenant architectures with differentiated policies for privacy, retention, or purpose.
How can be implemented?:
Define data usage policies:
• Rules such as: “data type X may only be processed by module Y between 08:00–18:00 if location = BR and trust level ≥ 0.8.”
• Use declarative formats such as OPA (Open Policy Agent), Rego, or XACML.

Adopt secure middleware with contextual control:
• Eclipse ioFog, Zenoh, DDS Secure, gRPC interceptors, NATS with JetStream + policy engine.
• Intercepts, applies rules, and encrypts/filters data dynamically based on context.

Implement end-to-end encryption and sensitivity labeling:
• Example: AES-GCM protected stream, with each message carrying classification/sensitivity metadata.

Audit and active enforcement:
• Signed access logs, flow blocking upon policy violation, or real-time resolution/sampling downgrade.
Is there any other viable way?:
• TLS alone — secures the communication channel but does not prevent improper reuse once the data reaches its destination.

• Document-based policies (e.g., SLAs, Terms of Service) — lack technical enforcement and do not prevent actual misuse.

The combination of a policy engine, secure middleware, end-to-end encryption, and contextual metadata provides real and adaptive protection.
Are there any practical examples?:
DDS Secure allows configuring governance documents with access policies based on domain, topology, and data type.

    OPA is used with NATS or gRPC to enforce conditional policies (e.g., blocking access from services outside a trusted cluster or with low trust scores).

    In EdgeAIBench, sensitive data from ICU or Smart Home scenarios can be protected by controlling who consumes it, when, and under which conditions — simulating contextual enforcement.

    Zenoh implements dynamic filters and fine-grained control with plugins that integrate policies at publish/subscribe time.

Guidelines: Implement automatic device registration and discovery mechanisms integrated with centralized management platforms.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Facilitate the scalable and secure provisioning of new devices through automatic discovery and registration mechanisms integrated into a central management platform. This reduces manual effort, accelerates onboarding, maintains configuration consistency, and enables global control over the Edge environment.
What's problem does it address?:
"Manual registration processes are error-prone, slow, and unfeasible at scale (e.g., thousands of IoT sensors)."

"The absence of automated discovery complicates orchestration and monitoring, preventing dynamic control and real-time auditing."

"Devices may be connected inconsistently, without a unified policy or central traceability."
In what context is it applicable?:
In EdgeAI architectures with multiple devices dynamically connecting (sensors, actuators, gateways, cameras, etc.)."

"In industrial, urban, or federated environments that require central governance, even with distributed topologies."

"In projects requiring automatic provisioning, on-demand reconfiguration, or rapid hardware replacement."
How can be implemented?:
Automatic discovery mechanisms:
• mDNS / DNS-SD (Zeroconf), SSDP (UPnP), CoAP discovery, MQTT retained topics.
• Protocols with presence announcements (heartbeat + metadata).

Automatic registration with identity control:
• Device sends identity + metadata → management platform validates → response with config/token.
• Integration with membership services such as AWS IoT Core, KubeEdge, BalenaCloud, Open Horizon.

Integration with central platform:
• Backend receives discovery/onboarding events and applies policies for configuration, labeling, visibility, and security.

Identity verification before acceptance:
• Device attestation, fingerprinting, certificate, PSK, or signature.
Is there any other viable way?:
• Manual registration or CLI-based scripting — feasible only in small or controlled environments.

• Discovery without integration into the central platform — enables visibility, but lacks control and governance.

Integration with a central platform, combined with secure automated registration, represents the most robust and scalable model.
Are there any practical examples?:
KubeEdge uses EdgeController and DeviceTwin for automatic discovery and management of devices connected to edge nodes.

    Balena allows devices to self-enroll in specific projects using tokens and receive remote configuration after the first boot.

    AWS IoT Device Provisioning automates registration and assignment of policies/configurations based on device identity or hardware fingerprint.

    In EdgeAIBench, onboarding of nodes and sensors is simulated at scale, reflecting the use of dynamic discovery in experimental environments.

Guidelines: Implement centralized solutions to automate the orchestration and configuration of numerous edge devices across distributed environments.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Provide a centralized and automated control plane capable of orchestrating the full lifecycle of multiple Edge devices — including service deployment, updates, reconfigurations, and monitoring — thereby ensuring consistency, scalability, and efficient governance in heterogeneous and distributed environments.
What's problem does it address?:
"Manually managing distributed devices is unfeasible at scale and highly error-prone."

"Edge environments often present diversity in hardware, connectivity, and regional requirements — hindering uniform configurations without automation."

"The absence of centralized orchestration prevents the efficient rollout of updates, security policies, and policy-based reconfigurations."
In what context is it applicable?:
"In environments with a large number of heterogeneous Edge devices, such as factories, smart cities, or distributed healthcare systems."

"When coordinated response to changes is required (e.g., reconfiguring all devices in case of a new policy, failure, or event)."

"In architectures operating under continuous update cycles (AI models, firmware, business logic, communication routes)."
How can be implemented?:
Adopt edge-aware orchestration platforms:
• KubeEdge, Open Horizon, BalenaCloud, AWS Greengrass, Portainer Edge Agent, Azure IoT Edge.

Declare desired state and enable automatic reconciliation:
• YAML manifests, JSON files, or declarative dashboards.
• The orchestrator detects drift and reconciles the state (deploy, stop, update).

Group devices by profiles and apply batch configurations:
• Example: group “edge-cam-Salvador” → receives model_v2 and pipeline update.

Manage connectivity and dependencies:
• Status monitoring, fallback, asynchronous commands (e.g., MQTT, NATS, WebSockets).

Integrate security and access control policies per module/node.
Is there any other viable way?:
• Automation scripts (e.g., Ansible, shell) are useful, but lack real-time monitoring and state reconciliation.

• Manual tools or local dashboards may be suitable for small projects, but do not scale securely or with traceability.

Centralized orchestration enables consistency, operational efficiency, and integration with DevOps and observability practices.
Are there any practical examples?:
KubeEdge synchronizes the state of Kubernetes pods, devices, and volumes with edge nodes — enabling full declarative management.

    BalenaCloud applies OTA updates to multiple edge devices with automatic rollback in case of failure.

    IBM Edge Application Manager (Open Horizon) automates workload deployment with policy rules based on location, device type, and connectivity.

    EdgeAIBench uses configurable orchestration scenarios to simulate different workload distributions and coordinated reactions to events, reinforcing the importance of unified control in experimental environments.

Guidelines: Implement connection lifecycle tracking through standardized birth/death messages to monitor Edge device availability.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Ensure continuous visibility into the presence and availability of Edge devices over time through standardized messages that signal system entry (“birth”) and exit (“death”) — thereby enabling proactive failure detection, availability auditing, and automated responses to connectivity events.
What's problem does it address?:
"The absence of a formal presence mechanism makes it difficult to determine whether a device is active, inactive, or experiencing a silent failure."

"Failures may go unnoticed, undermining data reliability and decisions based on missing inputs."

"Continuous monitoring based solely on polling or logs is neither efficient nor scalable."
In what context is it applicable?:
In any EdgeAI architecture with multiple devices that dynamically connect and disconnect.

In solutions requiring high availability, reliability, or real-time decision-making (e.g., control, monitoring, continuous inference).

In environments where auditing the historical presence of devices is relevant (e.g., compliance, SLA, diagnostics).
How can be implemented?:
Define standard birth/death messages:
• Birth Message: sent at startup or reconnection; contains ID, device type, timestamp, version, etc.
• Death Message: sent before shutdown or after a heartbeat timeout.

Use event-driven communication channels:
• MQTT, NATS, DDS, ZeroMQ, WebSockets.
• Topics such as status/{device_id}/birth and status/{device_id}/death.

Heartbeat as fallback:
• If no explicit death message, configure a timeout (e.g., 60s without heartbeat = disconnected).

Log events and trigger responses:
• Update dashboards, send notifications, reconfigure routing logic, or replace nodes.
Is there any other viable way?:
• Continuous polling of each device’s state — inefficient and prone to false positives or negatives.

• Indirect traffic monitoring (e.g., logs, metrics) — may not accurately reflect actual presence.

Birth/Death messages are simple, efficient, and compatible with asynchronous and reactive architectures.
Are there any practical examples?:
Sparkplug B (MQTT specification) formally defines NBIRTH, NDEATH, DBIRTH, and DDEATH messages for devices and nodes — with standardized payloads.

    KubeEdge maintains a heartbeat connection between cloud and edge; absence of response triggers a disconnected event.

    Eclipse ioFog sends periodic presence signals and uses planned death messages before scheduled shutdowns.

    In EdgeAIBench, node join and leave events can be simulated — these lifecycle events can be tracked via messages for experimental reliability and robustness studies.

Guidelines: Adopt digital twin architectures to model and manage the identity, status, and behavior of Edge devices in real time, enabling intelligent capabilities and seamless cloud integration.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Enable each Edge device to be digitally represented by a dynamic virtual model (Digital Twin) that reflects its identity, state, and behavior in real time, serving as an integration point between Edge and cloud and enabling intelligent reasoning, continuous monitoring, and secure remote control.
What's problem does it address?:
"Without an updated virtual model, it is difficult to understand the current state of distributed devices, especially when they are offline or intermittently connected."

"The lack of a unified digital interface for each device undermines interoperability, automation, and integration with AI/ML applications."

"Real-time read/write operations performed directly at the Edge create strong coupling and hinder centralized control."
In what context is it applicable?:
In Edge–Cloud architectures where devices must be remotely monitored, controlled, or simulated.

In industrial, urban, or healthcare environments where the lifecycle management of physical assets must be traceable and auditable.

In solutions requiring integration with predictive models, centralized control dashboards, or state/condition-based logic.
How can be implemented?:
Create a digital representation for each device:
• Unique ID, type, current status (online, failure, etc.), properties (configuration, sensors), allowed commands, history.

Synchronize state between Edge and Twin:
• Edge sends updates (pull/push); Twin may issue commands (write-back).
• Use brokers (e.g., MQTT, DDS, NATS) or REST/gRPC APIs.

Integrate with digital twin platforms:
• Azure Digital Twins, AWS IoT TwinMaker, Eclipse Ditto, or custom frameworks.

Enable simulation, reconfiguration, and AI:
• The Twin can feed predictive models, simulate failures, or anticipate maintenance.

Associate identity and access control with the Twin:
• The twin acts as a proxy for authorization, tracking, and governance.
Is there any other viable way?:
• Monitoring state directly through logs or metrics — does not provide full context or support for high-level reasoning.

• Managing devices via direct commands — leads to tight coupling and hinders abstraction, versioning, or simulation.

The Digital Twin is the ideal modern abstraction for intelligent, interoperable, and controllable Edge Computing.
Are there any practical examples?:
Azure Digital Twins provides a graph representation of devices with status and relationships, integrating with edge sensors via IoT Hub.

    Eclipse Ditto enables creating digital “things” synchronized with physical devices through MQTT, REST, or WebSockets.

    In EdgeAIBench, scenarios with simulated or partially connected devices can be managed using digital twins — facilitating testing, logging, and intelligent orchestration.

    ROS 2 integrated with digital twins allows robots to continuously publish their state and be monitored or controlled by cloud-aware systems.

Guidelines: Use declarative configurations (e.g., ConfigMaps) and edge-side agents to orchestrate network plugins, load balancing rules, and secure tunnels.
What's the purpose of the guideline?: Enable programmable, reproducible, and secure control of network configuration in Edge devices through local agents that interpret declarative configurations to enforce routing, balancing, and security policies — thereby promoting automation, consistency, and operational flexibility.
What's problem does it address?:
"Manual network configurations are fragile, non-traceable, and difficult to scale in distributed Edge environments."

"Without local agents, rules do not persist across reboots or adapt to real-time changes."

"The absence of declarative orchestration makes the system less transparent and prevents the automatic reconciliation of the desired state."
In what context is it applicable?:
In Edge systems that require load balancing, dynamic routing, tunneling, or local firewall policies.

In environments with multiple autonomous or semi-autonomous Edge devices that must maintain network consistency even when offline.

In solutions with a centralized control plane but decentralized execution via local agents.
How can be implemented?:
Use declarative configurations (YAML, JSON):
• Example: Kubernetes ConfigMaps, .conf files, or versionable custom schemas.
• Declare: load-balancing rules, routes, VPN peers, allowed ports and protocols.

Run edge-side agents as reconcilers:
• Read configurations, apply rules, and monitor state.
• Examples: cilium-agent, Envoy sidecar, Open vSwitch agent, or custom agents in Python/Go.

Synchronize with control plane or broker:
• Pull or push updates via MQTT, HTTP, GitOps, etc.

Manage secure tunnel rules dynamically:
• WireGuard configurations, NAT rules, peer control based on policies or context.
Is there any other viable way?:
Yes, but with limitations:

• Shell scripts — fragile, hardly reusable, and lacking declarative traceability.

• Manual configuration — impractical at scale and carries high operational risk.

• Push-only remote control — sacrifices reactivity and local flexibility.

The declarative model with local agents enables resilience, observability, and true automation.
Are there any practical examples?:
KubeEdge allows configuring ConfigMaps synchronized with agents on the edge, which apply network rules, QoS, or proxy settings.

    Cilium uses eBPF and declarative configuration to enforce network policies and load balancing with full visibility.

    Nebula (a VPN mesh) uses YAML files to orchestrate private networks among edge nodes, with ACLs and routes configured by agents.
